summary: Eastham's Three Sisters, 1838, then the 1877 Chatham cast-iron tower moved here in 1923. Moved 300 feet from the eroding bluff in 1996; now relit and open for tours.

access.note: Tower open for scheduled tours; grounds reached by a path from a parking lot off Ocean View Drive.

stay.note: Keeper's house offered as a short-term rental by the Nauset Light Preservation Society from June 2024

facts.agency: Nauset Light Preservation Society (operates the light for the Cape Cod National Seashore)

events.note: Three brick towers, about 15 feet tall and 150 feet apart (the Three Sisters)
Station established with stationary lamps
Isaac Dunham, first head keeper on the LighthouseFriends list, to 1842
Sixth-order Fresnel lenses with valve lamps replace the original lamps
Fourth-order lenses replace the sixth-order lenses at the Three Sisters
Second keeper's house built (LighthouseFriends dates the dwelling to 1876)
Cast-iron twin tower built at Chatham, 48 feet tall; the north tower was moved to Eastham in 1923
Three movable wooden towers, about 30 feet west of the old towers, replace the brick towers after erosion; lights raised 4 feet, April 25, 1892
Oil house (brick, slate roof)
Nauset station patrol finds lumber and wreckage drifting ashore about a mile north of the Nauset Beach Beacons; no vessel seen
Center tower fitted with a revolving Fresnel lens, triple flash; the tower becomes known as The Beacon
Northern tower of the Chatham twin lights moved to Eastham in seven sections, about 200 feet from the cliff edge, replacing the last wooden tower
20,000-candle-power kerosene lamp installed in the fourth-order Fresnel lens
Last wooden tower (The Beacon) sold at public auction to a private buyer
Top half of the iron tower painted red as a daymark
Electric lamp and automation; keeper no longer needed; keeper's house sold. LighthouseFriends dates automation to 1955
National Park Service buys two of the three old wooden towers
Fourth-order Fresnel lens replaced by two rotating aerobeacons; removed lens now at the Salt Pond Visitor Center
Signal changed from three white flashes to one red and one white flash, five seconds apart
Cape Cod National Seashore restores the Three Sisters in their original configuration in a park off Cable Road
Tower about 50 feet from the cliff; Coast Guard declares it surplus and darkens it; Nauset Light Preservation Society founded November 10, 1993
Coast Guard grants an operation and maintenance lease to the Nauset Light Preservation Society
Tower and oil house moved intact about 300 feet across the road, November 15-16, 1996; cost $330,000 per the Society (LighthouseFriends gives 336 feet from the bluff)
Relit as a private aid to navigation on May 10; ownership transferred from Coast Guard to National Park Service
Keeper's house moved across the road to stand beside the tower, October 1998
Tower repainted
Rust removed and tower repainted
Keeper's house transferred to the National Park Service, April 2024

corrections.current: tower, cast_iron, cast_iron, built 1838, 15.0 m, standing
corrections.proposed: tower, cast_iron, built 1877 at Chatham, moved to Eastham 1923; 14.6 m (48 ft)
corrections.why: The 1838 Three Sisters were three brick towers, lost to erosion and replaced in 1892 by wooden towers. The cast-iron tower standing now dates from 1877 at Chatham and was moved to Eastham in 1923.

corrections.proposed: 1923 lit at Eastham (fourth-order lens with kerosene lamp); 1877 built at Chatham
corrections.why: The 1877 tower was lit at Chatham. At Nauset, the current tower was first lit in 1923 after the move (NPS, LighthouseFriends, Society timeline).

corrections.proposed: 1993 deactivated (darkened); 1997 relit as private aid to navigation
corrections.why: The Coast Guard darkened the light in 1993 and declared it surplus. It was relit on May 10, 1997, as a private aid, after the move.

corrections.proposed: ownership federal (National Park Service) since May 10, 1997; operated by the Nauset Light Preservation Society
corrections.why: The Society timeline says ownership of the light passed from the Coast Guard to the National Park Service in 1997. The Society operates it under agreement.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Three Sisters were three brick towers from 1838. The tower now standing is the cast-iron 1877 tower built at Chatham and moved to Eastham in 1923. The record's 1838 date applies to the station, not to this tower.

The Massachusetts survey form, NPS and the Society timeline agree the 1981 change replaced the fourth-order Fresnel lens with aerobeacons, and that the removed lens is at the Salt Pond Visitor Center. LighthouseFriends names it a Barbier and Benard lens; the Society timeline calls it the existing fourth-order lens.

notes_for_editor: 1) The 1838 Three Sisters were brick; the standing tower is the 1877 cast-iron Chatham tower moved to Eastham in 1923 (MHC, NPS, Society, LighthouseFriends). The record's 'built 1838 cast_iron' is wrong; see corrections. 2) Characteristic: the record says Al Fl W R 10s; the 1981 change (NPS, Society, MHC, LighthouseFriends) gives alternating red and white flashes five seconds apart. Not established which is current; not used in facts. 3) Focal height: the Society timeline gives 114 ft (34.7 m) above mean high water in 1981; the record gives 36.6 m. Range: the record 24 nm; the Society 17 miles (1981); the survey form 19 miles (1981). Not used. 4) Lens: LighthouseFriends names a Barbier and Benard lens; the Society calls it an existing fourth-order lens; both say 4th order at Salt Pond now. 5) Dwelling date: the survey form and the Society say 1875; LighthouseFriends says 1876. 6) Automation: the Society timeline says 1952; LighthouseFriends says 1955. 7) Herbolt: LighthouseFriends 1919 to 1932; US Lighthouse Society archive 1929 to 1932. 8) James Yates shares a name with a West Chop keeper in the archive; no source read connects them. 9) Benjamin H.A. Collins appears as a keeper and as seller of the site in 1838; no source read connects them. 10) Nathan A. Gill Sr./Jr. are listed with no relationship given. 11) The 1887 wreckage entry is from the Life-Saving Service report for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1888; the date November 1, 1887 is derived from the fiscal year. 12) Distance of the 1996 move: 300 feet across the road (NPS, Society) vs 336 feet from the bluff (LighthouseFriends). 13) The 1924 sale: the Society says the last wooden tower sold at public auction to Albert and Mary Hall; LighthouseFriends says the remaining Sister was sold for $10 to Albert Hall. Not in the story. 14) LighthouseFriends is an all-rights-reserved site and the Society's timeline is copyrighted: facts were paraphrased and short phrases quoted. 15) Private owners of the keeper's house are not named. 16) No Life-Saving Service narrative tied the keeper's wreck to the light beyond the 1887 entry; the 1893 Ada K. Damon narrative names the Nauset station but its month and location were not confirmed, so it is not used. 17) Fact-check 2026-10-22: the seven assistants on LighthouseFriends's list (1867-1882) are now in the roster with cite 3. 18) Focal height: the Society's timeline gives 114 ft (34.7 m) above mean high water for 1981, used in facts; the USLHS record gives 102 ft (31.1 m) above mean high water, not reconciled. 19) The 1887 wreckage entry is dated November 1 in the report for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1888 (scan 166), so the year 1887 follows from the fiscal year. 20) The 1892 tower move is in the report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1892 (scan 341), dated April 25, 1892.
